intro: The same moments appear in almost every theory, under different names. The alignment is approximate: each thinker slices the story a little differently, and some don't follow the arc at all.

moments.title: The world before
moments.gloss: Life before the story starts. Who these people are and what normal looks like.

moments.title: Disruption
moments.gloss: The event that knocks life off balance and gives someone something to want.

moments.title: Rising complications
moments.gloss: Pursuit of the goal meets resistance, and each obstacle costs more than the last.

moments.title: Midpoint turn
moments.gloss: A shift in the middle: a false victory, a false defeat, or a change of direction.

moments.title: Lowest point
moments.gloss: Everything seems lost, and the hardest choice has to be made.

moments.title: Climax
moments.gloss: The decisive confrontation or action. The story's question is answered.

moments.title: New normal
moments.gloss: The aftermath. What has changed, and what it means.

setup.g: What needs nothing before it to make sense.

rising.g: Everything from the start up to the turn in fortune.

climax.g: Peripeteia and anagnorisis: fortune turns as ignorance becomes knowledge. Best when they coincide, as in Oedipus.

resolution.g: From the turn to the end. It should come from the plot itself, not a deus ex machina.

frameworks.name: Freytag
frameworks.note: Freytag's 'climax' sits in the middle of the play, not near the end. It's the hero's high point, after which fortune falls.

disruption.g: The moment that sets the action going.

rising.g: Complications build toward the high point.

midpoint.g: The peak of the pyramid, at the center of a five-act play.

crisis.g: The downward turn, with one last moment of hope that escape is possible.

climax.g: In tragedy, the hero's downfall. It also ends the play.

disruption.g: Followed by Refusal of the Call and Meeting with the Mentor.

rising.t: Crossing the Threshold · Tests, Allies, Enemies · Approach
rising.g: Into the special world, learning its rules, nearing the inmost cave.

midpoint.g: A central brush with death, and the prize it wins.

crisis.g: Consequences pursue the hero; a recommitment to finishing the journey.

climax.g: A final, most dangerous test where the hero proves what they've learned.

resolution.g: Home again, carrying something that changes the ordinary world.

setup.g: Roughly the first quarter, pages 1–30 of a 120-page script.

disruption.g: Plot Point I, around page 25–27, spins the story into Act II.

rising.g: The long middle: obstacles to the dramatic need.

midpoint.g: Added in his later books: a turn around page 60 that splits Act II.

crisis.g: Around page 85–90, spins the story into Act III.

setup.g: Life in relative balance before the story.

disruption.g: Radically upsets that balance and creates an object of desire.

rising.g: Widening gaps between expectation and result, to a point of no return.

midpoint.g: A major reversal. McKee counts acts by these, not by a fixed template.

crisis.g: A dilemma: irreconcilable goods or the lesser of two evils. Character is revealed in the choice.

climax.g: The action that results. Absolute, irreversible change.

disruption.g: Catalyst at page 12; the hero hesitates until page 25.

rising.t: Break into Two · B Story · Fun and Games
rising.g: Pages 25–55: 'the promise of the premise'.

midpoint.g: Page 55: a false victory or false defeat, and the stakes go up.

crisis.t: Bad Guys Close In · All Is Lost · Dark Night of the Soul
crisis.g: Pages 55–85, with a 'whiff of death' at All Is Lost.

resolution.g: A mirror of the Opening Image, showing the change.

setup.g: A character is in a zone of comfort…

rising.g: They enter an unfamiliar situation and adapt to it.

frameworks.name: Jon Franklin
frameworks.note: Franklin folds the climax and its aftermath into a single resolution.

setup.g: A real person the reader can follow.

disruption.g: Something happens that complicates their life.

rising.g: Often three, each a short active statement.

climax.g: The character's own action, often an insight, resolves the complication.

frameworks.name: Kishōtenketsu
frameworks.note: Four parts, and no conflict required. The twist is a surprising new element or angle, not a confrontation.

rising.g: The situation deepens, without opposition.

resolution.g: We see how the twist and what came before fit together.

frameworks.name: The inverted pyramid
frameworks.note: Doesn't map onto the arc at all. Facts are ordered by importance, not time: who, what, when, where, why first, so a reader can stop anywhere and an editor can cut from the bottom.

frameworks.name: The Nāṭyaśāstra
frameworks.note: Five stages of the hero's action, each paired with a juncture of the plot. Built toward attaining a goal and a happy ending, not tragic catastrophe.

disruption.g: Beginning: eagerness for the result. The seed (bīja) of the action is planted.

rising.g: Effort: striving toward the goal.

midpoint.g: Possibility of attainment: success is in sight, obstacles remain.

crisis.g: A juncture of doubt and deliberation, after which success becomes certain.

climax.g: Attainment of the result, the fruit of the action.

resolution.g: The conclusion: threads gathered, often closing with a benediction.

frameworks.name: Zeami's jo-ha-kyū
frameworks.note: A theory of tempo and intensity, not conflict. It applies at every scale, from a gesture to a day's program.

setup.g: A slow, simple, calm opening that lets the audience settle.

rising.g: The longest part: the opening is broken open and things grow more complex and intense.

frameworks.name: Lajos Egri
frameworks.note: Egri builds from a premise and from character; this is the shape his conflict takes once the characters are set going.

disruption.g: Begin where something is at stake and a decision sets the conflict going.

rising.g: Step-by-step transitions move characters from one pole toward its opposite.

crisis.g: The conflict comes to a head between opponents bound by a unity of opposites.

climax.g: The outcome that proves the premise.

resolution.g: The aftermath, with the characters changed.

frameworks.name: Vladimir Propp
frameworks.note: Drawn from Russian wonder tales. Not every tale has every function, and many have a second move, so the fit with the arc is loose.

setup.g: Not a function: the family or the hero introduced. Then absentation, interdiction, violation.

disruption.g: Someone is harmed or something is missing, and the hero is sent out.

rising.g: The hero leaves home, is tested by a donor and receives a magical agent.

midpoint.g: Hero and villain fight; the villain is defeated and the lack put right.

crisis.g: On the way home the hero is chased; an impostor claims the credit and a hard task is set.

climax.g: The task is done, the true hero recognized, the false hero unmasked.

resolution.g: The villain is punished; the hero marries and takes the throne.

frameworks.name: Jack Hart
frameworks.note: For story narratives only. Hart's explanatory narratives and vignettes don't need the full arc.

setup.g: Introduce the protagonist and their world.

disruption.g: The problem the protagonist must confront, as in Franklin.

rising.g: A series of plot points, each turning the story in a new direction.

crisis.g: The struggle comes to a head; the protagonist sees the situation in a new way.

climax.g: The complication is resolved, often through that insight.

resolution.g: The denouement: loose ends tied up.

frameworks.name: John Truby
frameworks.note: Truby rejects three-act structure. His seven steps track the hero's inner change as much as the plot.

setup.g: The hero's flaw, and what they must fulfil to live better. Usually unknown to them.

disruption.g: A specific goal in the world. Desire drives the plot; need drives the change.

rising.g: An opponent who wants the same goal, and the hero's strategy to beat them.

crisis.g: One of his 22 steps, not the seven: the hero seems beaten.

climax.g: The final conflict decides who gets the goal, and through it the hero sees past their weakness.

resolution.g: Back to normal, but the hero is at a higher, or in tragedy lower, level.

frameworks.name: Frank Daniel's sequences
frameworks.note: Each sequence is a little film with its own tension. Eight is typical for a two-hour feature; the count varies.

disruption.g: By the end of Act I, the film's overarching dramatic question is set up.

rising.g: The first half of Act II, each sequence with its own goal and question.

midpoint.g: The turn between Act II's two halves.

crisis.g: The second half of Act II, building to the turn that ends the act.

climax.g: Act III: the main tension is resolved.

frameworks.name: Kristin Thompson
frameworks.note: Found by timing real films: four parts of roughly equal length in a two-hour feature, divided by turning points where the protagonist's goals change.

setup.g: Characters, world and the protagonist's goals, often more than one.

disruption.g: About a quarter of the way in, it creates a new situation.

rising.g: Goals may be redefined. Almost a second setup.

midpoint.g: Near the halfway mark: a full structural break, not an add-on.

crisis.g: The struggle toward the goals, with delays, obstacles and subplots, ending in a turn toward the end.

climax.g: The goals are clearly achieved or clearly lost.

frameworks.name: John Yorke
frameworks.note: Five acts, mirrored around the midpoint: Act Four echoes Act Two, Act Five echoes Act One. The same shape repeats inside each act and scene.

setup.t: Act One: the world and the flaw
setup.g: A protagonist with something lacking, in a familiar world.

disruption.g: The inciting incident pushes them toward the woods.

rising.g: First steps into the unfamiliar; early progress, doubts overcome.

midpoint.g: The heart of the woods: a crucial truth glimpsed, or a prize that isn't enough. The story turns.

crisis.g: Opposition mounts and the old self fights back, ending in crisis.

climax.g: The protagonist must act on what they've learned.

frameworks.name: The story spine
frameworks.note: Born in improv theater and popularized by a Pixar story artist's tweets. Coats's version stops at 'Until finally'.

setup.t: Once upon a time… Every day…

rising.t: Because of that… Because of that…
rising.g: Each event must cause the next, not just follow it.

climax.g: The event the chain has been building toward.

resolution.g: Kenn Adams's closing line: the new normal.

frameworks.name: The well-made play
frameworks.note: Scribe wrote no manual; these features were reconstructed by later critics, notably Stephen Stanton (1957).

setup.g: The past laid out early, often by servants or old friends, with the secret planted.

rising.g: The hero's fortunes swing back and forth, driven by letters, misunderstandings and arrivals.

climax.g: The promised confrontation, where the secret comes out before the person who most needs to hear it.

frameworks.name: David Ball
frameworks.note: A method for reading plays: every event is a trigger for the next, and the chain should survive being read backwards.

setup.g: A state of balance, not necessarily a happy one.

disruption.g: Something upsets the stasis and releases forces that collide.

rising.g: Each event causes or permits the next, like falling dominoes, with forwards keeping the audience hungry for next.

resolution.g: The forces are no longer in conflict, and the play ends.
